With the fujara, another Slovak overtone herding flute, it belongs to the same shepherd-music context; in the wider context of European folk flutes it can be grouped with the Scandinavian willow flute as an overtone folk flute. A beginner can first steady the breath, practise opening and closing the foot hole and controlling the air speed, then build melodies from the partial Lydian scale the instrument offers.
Koncovka 為無指孔的氣鳴笛，音高來自尾端開閉與吹氣速度所切換的兩組泛音列: The koncovka is an aerophone without fingerholes; its pitch comes from two harmonic series, switched by the open or closed foot and by the speed of the breath, and with the foot open or closed a higher air speed reaches different harmonics. Traditional melodies use the partial Lydian scale the instrument can reach, so its range is not set by a layout of fingerholes but limited by the harmonic series and the state of the foot. Compared with the fujara and the willow flute, also overtone flutes, the koncovka's main feature is that it uses no fingerholes and changes pitch by opening and closing the foot.
